import Mathlib.Data.Finset.Basic

def s : Finset Nat := {1,2,3}
#eval s
-- could not synthesize a `ToExpr`, `Repr`, or `ToString` instance for type Finset ℕ

Why can't Finsets be printed? I would expect it to behave similarly to how printing a List or Vector works.

import Mathlib is heavy, it causes files to be slow in my experience. Which file specifically is the toString defined?

My next question is why this isn't shipped with Finset.Basic itself?

OK so import Mathlib.Data.Finset.Sort is what I needed. And it looks like if I import Sort, I don't need to import Basic.

I'm new to Lean, could anyone explain to me what's going on here?

@Marvin Repr is basically an instruction of how to eval something, so until you import that instruction you won't be able to eval; and sort imports basic so if you import sort you don't need to import basic

If you aren't familiar with the trait/type class concept, they're a programming abstraction for representing a common interface for multiple different types. docs#Repr is a type class that lets you define how a type is turned into a format, which is what's used to create the text of the eval.

Unlike many similar typeclass systems, Lean instances lack global coherence, meaning you can implement an instance for a given type multiple times. This is useful for the kinds of things Lean is used for, but has the side-effect of needing to import instances.

Also, imports in Lean can be marked as public, meaning that when you import a file, you also implicitly import that file's public imports. That's why importing Finset.Sort also imports Finset.Basic.

note that #eval is not the standard way to interact with Lean objects, and can easily be overridden, and this doesn't actually allow you to prove any false theorems so this isn't a bug

inductive Foo | a | b

#check Foo.a
#check Foo.b

instance : Repr Foo where reprPrec _ _ := repr 0

#eval Foo.a -- 0

I understand typeclasses and repr, I'm just confused why this isn't automatically included in the Basic import? Wouldn't we want to assume that if someone is using Finsets, they might want to print them?

And I'm confused why if I import Sort I no longer need to import Basic, what is the relationship there?

As for the imports: importing in Lean is transitive. So whenever you import A and that A imports B, then you no longer need to import B.

Now about Finset printing, here's my understanding of , some correct me if I am wrong please.

Note that the contents of a Finset are not ordered, so mathematically {1,2,3} and {3,2,1} are the same thing. But to make a Repr Finset instance we need one-and-only way to turn a Finset a value into a String. That is why the Repr Finset instance that gives us ths Finset-to-String conversion is defined via Finset.sort that first converts the Finset to a List so we have something that can be printed in a canonical way. But wait, for some types a we might not have an order at all, so then also those Finset a values cannot be turned into lists and cannot be printed.

As for why all this machinery is not in the Basic module: One can use Finsets in the sense of "proving stuff about them" without ever printing them and without ever needing Finset.sort etc. So I guess it's also just practical to not make Data.Finset.Basic too long of a file.

Lastly, if you still feel like "why such a big fuzz about this, how hard can it be to print something?" you may be happy to know that you can actually print the content of a Finset Int by using its internal representation: a Finset is a Multiset which in fact is already a List. See below.

import Mathlib.Data.Finset.Basic

def myfinset : Finset Int := {3,1,2,1}

-- #eval bla -- needs `Repr` instance

-- A Finset is internally a Multiset:
#check myfinset.val -- Multiset ℤ

-- Multiset is a Quotient, so we can use this:
#check Quot.unquot -- Quot.unquot {α} {r : α → α → Prop} : Quot r → α

-- So here is a way to print the list inside the multiset inside the finset:
#eval myfinset.val.unquot -- [3,2,1]

-- But that is unsafe because the *same* Finset will get printed differently:
def otherfinset : Finset Int := {1,2,3}
#eval otherfinset.val.unquot -- [1,2,3]

theorem same : myfinset = otherfinset := by grind [myfinset,otherfinset]
Confusingly, docs#Finset.instRepr is in the Sort module but the implementation of the Repr instance actually uses the .val.unquot trick and doesn't sort at all
Uhhh, well in that case what I wrote about was wrong speculation, sorry, I did not read the sources.

Malvin Gattinger said:

But wait, for some types a we might not have an order at all, so then also those Finset a values cannot be turned into lists and cannot be printed.

There is a trick: you can use the provided Repr instance to convert it into a Multiset Format, and those can be sorted.
Hmm there's this: mathlib3#18166. The obvious complaint about sorting by repr is that it is as bad as javascript at sorting numbers.

Marvin said:

Wouldn't we want to assume that if someone is using Finsets, they might want to print them?

Just to give you a counterpoint -- I use finsets a ton in my mathematical work and I have never wanted to print them. A lot of people here just want to prove theorems about them. I never use #eval in my work at all, in fact, I just focus on definitions and theorems about these definitions.
